sentences.text: Laquintasaura venezuelae is the only known species of this extinct dinosaur genus.
It was a small, lightly built animal that did not exceed one meter in length.
Prepared material included cranial remains, abundant teeth, various vertebrae, a scapula, and pelvic and hindlimb elements.
However, forelimb material was completely absent and foot material was very limited.
The creature possessed a bird-like hip bone and was likely a capable bipedal runner.
Its teeth were triangular with striations and sharp denticles, differing from the leaf-shaped teeth of related ornithischians.
The genus was formally described by Barrett and colleagues in 2014.
Laquintasaura is considered one of the most primitive ornithischians and the first dinosaur identified from Venezuela.
The generic name combines the La Quinta Formation with the Greek suffix for lizard.
The species is known from hundreds of fossil elements found in a single extensive bonebed.
The site was initially discovered by French paleontologists, with subsequent excavations largely led by Marcelo R Sánchez-Villagra.
Hundreds of fossil elements represent at least four individuals, possibly more.
Researchers suggest its unique teeth may have supported an omnivorous diet.
It likely lived in groups on seasonal alluvial plains and was preyed upon by Tachiraptor.
Bone histology analysis suggested one Laquintasaura tibia belonged to a juvenile approximately three years old.
Analysis of a scapula indicated it belonged to a mature Laquintasaura adult likely around ten to twelve years old.
Laquintasaura is robustly considered a basal member of Ornithischia, though its exact position within the group remains unresolved.
Some 2017 studies suggested Laquintasaura was a very early member of Thyreophora, as the sister taxon to Scutellosaurus.
A 2022 study placed Laquintasaura outside Prionodontia, intermediate between traditional Ornithischia and Silesauridae.
Laquintasaura lived during the Hettangian stage, from 201.4 to 199.5 million years ago.
There is a debate regarding whether it is an early diverging ornithischian or belongs to the subgroup Thyreophora.
Similar dental morphotypes found in India and England date to the Middle Jurassic, over 30 million years after Laquintasaura lived.
Conclusions about Laquintasaura's growth rates remain uncertain due to limited data and sample size.
